title: How do you stay calm when nerves hit in a case interview?
description: Practical, kind advice for staying calm before and during a case interview, and what to do in the moment when your mind goes blank.
hook: Almost everyone is nervous before a case interview. That is normal, and it is not a sign you are not ready. A bit of nerves can even help you focus. The aim is not to feel nothing; it is to have a few simple tools so that nerves do not take over. Here are the ones that work.
body:
Before the day

  • Practise out loud, with people. Nerves fade with familiarity. By your tenth case with a partner, the format itself stops being scary.
  • Practise recovering, not just succeeding. Ask partners to throw you a curveball sometimes, so getting stuck becomes familiar too.
  • Sleep beats cramming. A rested brain does maths and structures far better than a tired one with one extra framework in it.

On the day

  • Do a short 30-minute warm-up: something familiar, a voice warm-up, one easy mini-case.
  • Slow breathing helps. Breathing in for four counts and out for six, a few times, calms most people quickly.
  • Remind yourself the interviewer wants you to do well. They are hoping to hire someone today.

When your mind goes blank

It happens to strong candidates too. What matters is what you do next.

  1. Ask for a moment. "Could I take a few seconds to think about that?" Nobody minds.
  2. Go back to the goal. Look at the box at the top of your notes. What are we trying to achieve?
  3. Say what you know. "So far we know A and B. We're trying to get to C. So the next thing to check is..." Saying it out loud often unlocks the next step.

If you make a mistake

Correct it calmly and move on: "Sorry, I made an error there. It's 2.4 million, not 24 million, which changes the conclusion to..." Interviewers often care more about how you handle a mistake than whether you made one.

After the interview

Write down what went well and one thing to improve, then let it go. Replaying it all evening does not change the outcome, and you may have another interview tomorrow.

Practise the recovery, not just the perfect answer

Imagine you have calculated a 15% revenue decline and the interviewer points out that you used the wrong denominator. A weak response is to defend the calculation because you feel embarrassed. A stronger response is: "You're right, I used last year's volume but this year's price. I'll correct the baseline and check whether the conclusion changes." You have shown judgment by revising the analysis.

Build recovery into practice. Ask a partner to interrupt once with a contradictory fact. Allow yourself ten seconds to look at the client objective, restate what is known and propose the next test. Practise this until a correction no longer feels like the end of the case.

There is also a useful difference between silence while thinking and silence because you are lost. Ask for a moment before structuring. When you resume, give the interviewer the headline first. If you genuinely cannot reconcile two numbers, name the discrepancy and ask which definition is correct. Nobody expects a flawless recital; the interview is a test of how you work through uncertainty.
